title: the rich kid who gave his clothes back
hook: the rich kid who gave his clothes back
tomorrow: why there's fire in every church

segments.voice: Yesterday, the saints: not statues, people who fell and kept going. Your line was: the company you're in. Today we meet one of them up close. Day eight.

Italy, around the year 1200. A town on a hill called Assisi. There's a young man there everyone knows: the son of a rich cloth merchant, good clothes, good parties, the one who pays for everybody's dinner. He dreams of being a knight. He goes off to a war with the next town, gets captured, spends a year in a prison cell, and comes home sick. And something in him has changed. He starts giving things away. Money, cloth from his father's shop. His father is furious, and drags him in front of the bishop of Assisi, in the town square, to get his property back. What the son does next is why people still know his name.
screen: `ASSISI, AROUND 1200.` → `THE RICH MERCHANT'S SON.` → `DRAGGED BEFORE THE BISHOP.`

segments.voice: His name was Francesco. We say Francis. According to the stories written down by his early followers, he stood in front of the bishop and the whole town, took off his clothes, every piece, folded them, and handed them back to his father. And he said, in effect: until now I called you my father. From now on I'll say our Father, who art in heaven. The bishop covered him with his own cloak. Francis walked out of town with nothing. What came next is the part people forget. He didn't become a hermit. He went toward the people everyone avoided. The stories say that once, riding outside town, he met a man with leprosy, a disease that made people outcasts, and instead of riding past, he got down and kissed his hand. Later he wrote that what had seemed bitter to him was turned into sweetness. He rebuilt ruined chapels with his own hands. He gathered friends who lived poor, preached in the streets, and cared for the sick. They became the Franciscans, and there are still thousands of them today. He loved creation, too. Near the end of his life he wrote a song, the Canticle of the Creatures, praising God for brother sun and sister moon, even sister death. Now today's line: lord, make me an instrument. It opens the famous prayer that bears his name, make me an instrument of your peace. Here's the honest part. Francis almost certainly didn't write it. It first appeared in a small French magazine in 1912, seven centuries later. People attached his name because it sounds exactly like him. Which says a lot about the man.
screen: `HE GAVE THE CLOTHES BACK.` · `TOWARD THE PEOPLE EVERYONE AVOIDED.` · `BROTHER SUN, SISTER MOON.` · `THE PRAYER HE PROBABLY DIDN'T WRITE.` · then, large: `MAKE ME AN INSTRUMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A forty-five-second sit. Get comfortable and let your breath slow down. Think of one thing you own that you're holding on to a little too tightly. It doesn't have to be big. A grudge counts. With each breath out, imagine loosening your grip on it, the way Francis folded his clothes and handed them back. If you pray, you can say the line: lord, make me an instrument. The bell holds the time.
Francis. Francis of Assisi, the rich kid who gave it all back and went toward the outcasts. Eighth word.
Your line: lord, make me an instrument. Today, be the tool for one small good thing: carry something, fix something, make peace somewhere. Day eight.

screen: `DAY 8 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY THERE'S FIRE IN EVERY CHURCH.`

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Saint Francis on October 4, and many parishes bless pets and animals around that day; the Peace Prayer, though written in the twentieth century, is widely prayed in his name.

fork.setup: your furious father has dragged you before the bishop in the town square to get his property back. you're Francis. what do you do?
options: apologize and go back to the shop.
take off your clothes and hand them back.
fork.reveal: he gave back everything, down to his clothes, and said he'd now call only God our Father. the bishop covered him with his cloak.

original.note: Umbrian Italian, not Latin: praised be you, my Lord. the refrain of Francis's Canticle of the Creatures.

trapdoor: what you thought: the saint with the birds on the garden statue.
what it means: a rich merchant's son who gave everything back and went toward the outcasts.
what a scholar hears: the Canticle, among the earliest poems in Italian; the Peace Prayer, anonymous, first printed in La Clochette in 1912.

notes: Francis before the bishop and his words about 'Our Father who art in heaven' come from Thomas of Celano and Bonaventure; paraphrased. Confirm.
Kissing the leper's hand: from Celano/Bonaventure; his Testament says what seemed bitter was turned into sweetness. Paraphrased; confirm.
Capture after the war with Perugia (c. 1202) and about a year in prison; confirm.
The Peace Prayer's first known printing: La Clochette, Paris, 1912, anonymous. Confirm date and phrasing 'almost certainly didn't write it'.
The carry 'lord, make me an instrument' is the opening of the Peace Prayer; the index keeps it lowercase. Confirm it is fine to keep attributing it 'in his name' with the historical caveat.
